  - 🟡 **6. Shadows.** 1.15 ms of the 2.5 ms of GPU (45%) and 10,800 shadow draws for 2,350 scene draws in the measurement above; measurement of 2026-10-12 on the grid (release, SMAA, shadows "High", 16 full avatars, the GPU is the bottleneck): `g_shadows_depth` 2.39 ms of the 6.05 ms of GPU (0.38 ms with shadows off), 25,900 shadow draws for 3,750 scene draws. Cause: each cascade drew everything that fits in its square (wider than its slice of the view, so that its texels stay fixed), hence also what is behind the camera, beside the view, or too close to cast a shadow where that cascade is read; and all faces went through the shadow fragment shader (one texture read per fragment), even opaque ones. Done (`aurora-render/src/shadow_cull.rs`, `shaders/cull.wgsl`):
    - per-cascade culling: an object is drawn in a cascade only if its shadow can fall on what the view reads there — the volume of the pixels that read the cascade (the view, between the distances where `shadow_factor` uses it), stretched towards the light without limit; up to 12 planes per cascade, computed on the CPU, tested by the GPU culling (and by the CPU lists: terrain, fallback without `MULTI_DRAW_INDIRECT_COUNT`). Firestorm reaches the same objects by fitting each shadow frustum to the visible part of its slice (`LLPipeline::getVisiblePointCloud`). The shadow map only changes in texels that no pixel reads;
    - opaque faces drawn without a fragment shader (3 more bins in the GPU culling: per cascade, the opaque faces and the alpha-tested ones), like Firestorm's separate shadow programs; same depth;
    - cascade of a pixel chosen from its own distance to the camera, as the terrain and the water already did and like Firestorm (`sampleDirectionalShadow` reads the pixel's position), instead of the distance interpolated between the triangle's vertices. Without this no cascade has a nearest receiver (a pixel close to a large triangle read a far cascade) and the objects close to the camera stayed in all three cascades. **Only change to the image**, deliberate: on a triangle that spans several cascades (large floor, large wall), the boundary between cascades moves and the near shadows are sharper there; elsewhere the image is the same.
    - Measurements (demo, dev profile, 1600 × 900, MSAA 4x, 120 fps, old and new path alternated every second in the same session, medians; shared PC): `AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=3000` (3,000 textured objects around the camera) 23,850 → 6,580 shadow draws, `g_shadows_depth` 2.14 → 0.26 ms, GPU 4.36 → 2.32 ms; `AURORA_DEMO_TEXTURES=9000` 85,900 → 62,900 draws, 1.29 → 0.99 ms, GPU 3.37 → 2.80 ms; crowd of 40 avatars, 16 of them in full, each with a rigged mesh of 225,000 triangles (`AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=40`, `AURORA_DEMO_ANIMESH=1`, `AURORA_DEMO_ANIMESH_TRIS=200000`): 11.9 → 8.2 million shadow triangles per frame (5.4 with a high sun, `AURORA_DEMO_TOD=2`), 13,500 → 8,300 draws (5,100), `g_shadows_depth` 1.29 → 0.70 ms with a high sun (GPU 2.60 → 1.86 ms) and, depending on the load the other sessions were putting on the GPU (absolute times from 1 to 10 ms from one session to the next), 20 to 40% less with the demo's sun, 45 to 60% with a high sun; without an fps cap, with the GPU as the limit: 104 → 130 fps. Without the per-pixel choice of the cascade (`AURORA_SHADOW_LEGACY=splits`, pixel-identical image): 7,660 draws and 0.22 ms for the first scenario; for the crowd 12,200 draws and a time within the measurement noise, 8,900 draws and 0.80 ms with a high sun.
    - Image: screenshots of the old path (twice, to rule out what changes by itself: animations, clock), of `splits` and of the new one, in MSAA 4x and in SMAA (crowd, 9,000 cubes, plaza viewed towards the east, high and low sun, CPU lists). `splits`: identical to the old path, to within one level out of 255 on a few pixels at the edge of the animated avatars. New path: at most 8 levels of difference on 0.02 to 0.36% of the pixels, all on edges of shadows cast on large faces (plaza floor), at the boundary between two cascades, where the shadow is sharper. Tests: no point of the slice is in the shadow of a culled object (60,000 randomly drawn spheres, 300 views and lights), everything the view can read in a cascade is inside its volume, GPU bins equal to the CPU reference.
    - Profile: `g_shadows_depth` broken down (`g_cull`, `g_shadow0` to `g_shadow2`, `g_depth`), draws, triangles and share of rigged meshes per cascade (`sd`, `st_k`, `sd_rig`, `st_rig_k`). In the demo crowd, rigged meshes make up 99% of the shadow triangles for 5% of the draws, and the time follows the triangles (vertices): with nothing rasterised, the cascades cost only a quarter less. Comparison: `AURORA_SHADOW_LEGACY=1` (old path), `splits`, `ab` (the three paths in alternation, `shadow_path=` in `perf summary`).
    - Ruled out: small objects according to the size of their shadow (changes the image; objects smaller than 1.5 px on screen are already culled from the shadows); far cascade redrawn less often (its matrix changes as soon as the camera turns and the avatars move in it: it would take a cascade anchored to the world, with larger texels, hence a different image; the culling already empties it of what is near).
    - First trial by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12 (KB, release build combining this change, the sorted lights, the sync at rest and the hover; 88 s online in SMAA, shadows "High", ~27,700 objects, 62 posed skeletons): no defect spotted "on the fly", merge requested on that basis. Reading over the last 30 seconds, against the morning's release reading at the same place (24,880 objects, 52 skeletons: order of magnitude, the crowd is not the same): shadow draws 25,900 → 7,000, `g_shadows_depth` 2.39 → 1.15 ms, GPU 6.05 → 3.90 ms, 162 → 196 fps; the main thread becomes the limit again (`rt_idle` 2.2 ms, `wait_render` 0). Per cascade: 349 / 3,306 / 3,387 draws, 0.6 / 5.3 / 1.8 M triangles, 90% of them rigged meshes. Tests to complete on Agni: low sun and rotating sun, camera turned fast and in flight, shadows of objects out of view or behind you, BackBone Main Store, side by side with Firestorm; shadow edges between cascades to be judged with `AURORA_SHADOW_LEGACY=ab` (the three paths alternated every second: nothing must flicker outside these edges), measurement per path in the same session
    - ⬜ later: bound the receivers by what is really visible (prepass depth reduced per cascade in light space, with the transparent faces and the water) — the current volume goes down below the ground, which keeps in the first cascade objects whose shadow stops at the ground before reaching it when the sun is low; positions of the rigged meshes computed once per frame in compute and read back by the cascades, the prepass and the scene (the avatars' vertices are transformed five times per frame); `in_cascade` measures an object's radius with the first column of the cascade's matrix instead of its first row (radius underestimated at the edge of the square when the sun is low in the east or in the west, unchanged here).
    - ⬜ occlusion, later: shadow cascades (it would take a Hi-Z per cascade, that of the previous frame, or testing the cast shadow against the camera's Hi-Z) and reflections (quarter-resolution passes): GPU-only gain, whereas Aurora was limited by the CPU at the BackBone Main Store; to be taken up again if the shadows still weigh in `g_shadow0` to `g_shadow2` on the grid after the per-cascade culling of point 6 (no effect outdoors, where almost everything sees the sun; useful indoors). Also compact the main bins after the occlusion (it would take a second prefix sum to keep the order)
  - 🟡 **7. Depth prepass in MSAA.** First trial by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12 (KB, release build combining this change and the four previous ones, 68 s in MSAA 4x during the end of loading, 19,000 to 29,700 objects, 55 to 67 posed skeletons, `AURORA_MSAA_PREPASS=alt`): "good visually", merge requested on that basis. Reading, medians of the 22 periods without and of the 22 periods with the prepass: GPU 4.17 → 3.96 ms (−5%), objects 0.99 → 0.79 ms (−20%), terrain and sky 0.14 → 0.07 ms, prepass 0.06 ms; each period without the prepass compared with its two neighbours with it: 0.25 ms less in median, in 17 comparisons out of 17. The fps does not change in this place, limited by the main thread. Tests to complete on Agni: terrain at altitude (patches of sky through the ground), MSAA 2x and 8x, moving camera, fully loaded region and BackBone Main Store, edges of masked faces (foliage, hair).
    - 🟡 MSAA: the scene pass started again from an empty depth (no early-z); in demo, objects 0.63 ms in MSAA 4x against 0.17 ms without → prepass into the MSAA depth. With MSAA, the scene pass has its own multisampled depth and cannot reuse that of the single-sample prepass: a second prepass fills it just before (`renderer.rs`, `pre_msaa` pipelines, `vs_depth` without a fragment shader) with the terrain and the opaque faces — the very draws of the scene pass, same lists and same bins of the GPU culling after the occlusion, so the depth of each sample is the one the scene pass would have written — and the scene pass reuses it instead of clearing it. The alpha-masked faces are not in it: with MSAA their edge comes from `alpha to coverage`, which a depth pass cannot reproduce sample by sample; they are drawn after the opaque faces and were already tested against them. Nothing changes for the single-sample prepass (SSAO, water, Hi-Z, two-phase occlusion) nor for the other anti-aliasing modes. `AURORA_MSAA_PREPASS=0` keeps the old path; `alt` alternates the two (one second without, two with) and logs the median of the GPU times of each variant (`msaa prepass alt`); `perf summary` gives `g_depth` and `g_depth_msaa` separately, counted in `g_shadows_depth`; scenario `AURORA_DEMO_OVERDRAW=<n>` (opaque walls that overlap). **Cause confirmed where opaque surfaces overlap, not elsewhere**: in a scene with several planes the prepass removes about two thirds of what MSAA 4x added to the objects, in a scene without overlap it costs a little more than it saves. Measurements (shared RTX 4090, dev profile, 1600 × 900, capped at 120 fps, the two variants alternated in the same session, medians per variant, without the seconds when the card was taken by another process; GPU times in ms, without → with the prepass; "frame": sum of the items): local unversioned test scene (12,845 placed objects, no avatar, 4,303 draws, 876,000 triangles, buildings and meshes on several planes) in MSAA 4x: objects 0.505 → 0.359, terrain and sky 0.086 → 0.051, prepass 0.075, frame 1.525 → 1.417 (−7%); in MSAA 2x: objects 0.438 → 0.326, prepass 0.059, frame 1.426 → 1.339 (−6%); in MSAA 8x: objects 0.510 → 0.401, prepass 0.106, frame 1.603 → 1.557 (−3%); in SMAA, objects 0.288 and frame 1.246 in both variants (of the 0.22 ms that MSAA 4x added to the objects, 0.15 came from the overlap and 0.07 from the four samples). `AURORA_DEMO_OVERDRAW=12` (worst case): objects 0.501 → 0.258 (0.219 in SMAA), frame 1.054 → 0.786 (−25%). Demo alone: objects 0.225 → 0.208, terrain and sky 0.105 → 0.060, prepass 0.017, frame 0.713 → 0.667 (−6%). Crowd (`AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=40`, `AURORA_DEMO_ANIMESH=1`): objects 0.229 → 0.208, prepass 0.053, frame 0.828 → 0.831 (equal). Without overlap: `AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=3000` frame 0.865 → 0.895 (+3%); `AURORA_DEMO_TEXTURES=9000` with `AURORA_DEMO_OCCLUSION=1` 2.159 → 2.267 (+5%: 41,600 draws of which 36,400 hidden by the occlusion, which the prepass walks too as long as the main bins are not compacted after the occlusion, see point 6). The modes without MSAA (none, FXAA, TAA, SMAA) measure the same path twice and give the same time twice (demo in SMAA: frame 0.628 and 0.628). Identical image: the scene passes drawn twice in the same frame, without then with the prepass, and their resolved HDR colours compared texel by texel (19 scenes in MSAA 2x, 4x and 8x: demo, crowd and animesh, impostors, alpha masks and animated textures, PBR, flexible prims, altitude 2,085 and 3,900 m, SSR, CPU culling, without occlusion, local scene) differ only as two renders of the same path already differ from each other on this card (in the sky, a few units of the last digit of the 16-bit floats, in one frame out of ten to twenty); GPU validation with no error. Tests: `object_position_is_the_depth_prepass_position` and `prepass_and_scene_positions_are_invariant` (objects and terrain placed by the same operations as the prepass, `@invariant` positions), and a GPU test (`cargo test -p aurora-render prepass_depth -- --ignored`) that draws a simple face, two rigged meshes (placed by its record, by the anchor of its skeleton), an attached prim and terrain at 3,000 m of altitude through `vs_depth` then through `vs_main` / `vs_terrain` in 4 samples and compares the two depths sample by sample (it fails on 98,583 samples out of 182,262 if the terrain is put back in region coordinates). To validate on the grid: the original reading (release session of 2026-10-12, region of 24,880 objects, avatars included, 4.9 M triangles, `g_objects` 1.13 ms in SMAA and 2.05 in MSAA 4x) is reproduced by none of the offline scenes, which have neither its avatars nor its number of triangles; `AURORA_MSAA_PREPASS=alt` will give the real gain there. Later: sky tested against the prepass depth (0.03 ms less, but the last digit of the sky then changes in one frame out of five, ruled out to keep the image); same sky test without MSAA; masked faces in the MSAA prepass (the `alpha to coverage` would have to be replaced by a sample mask computed the same way in both passes, hence a change to the image); skip the prepass when the main bins contain mostly hidden draws.
  - ⬜ **8. Render thread and allocator.** Low priority as long as the render thread waits for the main thread (`rt_idle` 3.1 ms per frame in the reading).
    - ⬜ render thread, later: main-thread writes straight into staging memory (today copied into the write journal then copied again by wgpu on the render thread: `packet` 0.12–0.19 ms and `r_resources` 0.37 ms for 3.4 MB per frame in the demo crowd); CPU lists of the packet swapped instead of being copied (path without GPU culling); when rendering is the limit, start the main thread's frame later rather than waiting at the hand-off (latency); full screen and display scale change not tested in demo; placement of the render thread on the performance cores of hybrid processors to be measured with the window in the foreground; `r_finish` remains the render thread's largest cost
    - ⬜ texture pages, later: those of the textures created by a direct call (media, ban lines) are still created on the main thread (rare); the render thread still waits for `aurora-pages` when the allocator takes a block of video memory: this will only go away with render-thread writes through persistent buffers ("render thread, later" line), or with pages allocated outside wgpu's allocator
  - ⬜ **9. Reading on a modest card.** The measurements in this file come from RTX 3090 / 4090 cards. Redo the BackBone Main Store reading on a 6 to 8 GB card and on an integrated GPU (fps, "GPU time per pass", page memory): the order of points 1, 6 and 7 depends on it. Linked to the "Graphics quality levels according to the machine" line of "Rendering".
  - ⬜ Terrain LOD
  - 🟡 **GPU cost of transparent faces (`g_transparent`).** Release reading of 2026-10-12 at KB (24,880 objects, 52 posed avatars, 1278 × 1360, SMAA, GPU limiting at 6.05 ms per frame): `g_transparent` 1.55 to 1.67 ms for 318 transparent faces, second GPU item after the shadows, whereas the 3,750 opaque draws cost 1.13 ms.
    - what `g_transparent` measures: the sorted transparent faces, their interleaved glow, the debug and selection overlays, the particles and the end of the pass (in MSAA, the resolve); neither the water, nor the glow of opaque faces, nor the impostors. The GPU marks placed in a pass do not wait for the end of the work that precedes them: when these faces are heavy, part of their lighting is counted in `g_post`, more or less from one second to the next; the sum `g_transparent` + `g_post` is stable, and it is the one given below (docs/TESTING.md, Profiling).
    - what dominates, measured in demo: per-fragment lighting. Scene: `AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=40`, `AURORA_DEMO_HAIR=32` (966 transparent faces, 1.1 million triangles), `AURORA_DEMO_POS="129,134"`, 1278 × 1360, SMAA, cap of 120 fps, old light list; variants of the transparent faces' shader alternated every second in the same session (measurement code not kept). Sum of 0.77 to 0.96 ms depending on the run with the plaza's 8 lights, of which 0.18 ms without any shell. A constant colour in place of the shader: 0.21 ms; the textures without the lighting: 0.22 ms — fill, blending, vertices and textures make up only 7% of these faces' own cost, the lighting 93%. Without the walk over the local lights: −19%; without the 16 shadow taps: −23%; without both: −35%. With 64 lights (`AURORA_DEMO_LIGHTS=64`): 1.8 ms (up to 2.8 depending on the run), of which 62% for the light walk alone (0.69 ms without it) and 14% for the shadows.
    - what does not dominate: the triangles (8 layers, same area: 0.25 ms for 0.28 million transparent rigged triangles, 0.50 for 4.4 million, 1.00 for 15.6 million, i.e. +0.05 ms per million; the same triangles cost +0.28 ms per million in `g_shadows_depth`, 0.31 → 4.55 ms); the draws (one multi-draw per run of faces without glow). The cost follows the number of layers (8, 16, 32: 0.26, 0.36, 0.77 ms) and the size of the window (16 layers: 0.23 ms at 800 × 600, 0.36 at 1278 × 1360, 0.43 at 2400 × 1300).
    - on the grid, the light list was very probably full (64): not measured, inferred from `p_lights` (0.02 ms in the reading; 0.01 ms in demo for 72 light-emitting objects); the sky there was "classic" as in demo (same shader path). `lights=` and `blend_tris_k=` in "perf summary" will tell.
    - 🟡 local lights sorted by screen tile and by depth (`aurora-render/src/light_tiles.rs`): each lit fragment (transparent faces, opaque objects, terrain) walked the 64 lights of the list to find the few that reach it. The main view is cut into 32 columns, 32 rows and 32 depth slices; every frame the render thread computes, for each of them, the set of lights that cover it (816 bytes in the frame's uniforms), and a fragment only walks the lights common to its column, its row and its slice, in list order. Same image: a discarded light did not reach the fragment (the shaders add nothing outside the radius) and the others are summed in the same order. Reflections, probe faces and impostor snapshots keep the whole list. Measured in demo with 64 lights (scene above, `AURORA_LIGHT_TILES=alt`: old and new walk alternated every second, medians of 12 and 25 seconds): camera in front of the lights, in SMAA, GPU time of the frame 3.27 → 2.47 ms (−24%), transparent faces 1.89 → 1.21 ms (−36%), opaque objects −17%, terrain −25%; in MSAA 4x, 5.60 → 4.80 ms (−14%), transparent faces −22%. Camera in the middle of the lights (`AURORA_DEMO_POS="140,134"`): 5.90 → 4.49 ms (−24%) in SMAA, 5.84 → 4.78 ms (−18%) in MSAA 4x. With the plaza's 8 lights: 3.84 → 3.82 ms, nothing to gain or to lose.
    - 🟡 invisible fragments of transparent faces discarded before the lighting (alpha below 0.004), like Firestorm's `alphaF.glsl` / `pbralphaF.glsl` (`minimum_alpha`, LLDrawPoolAlpha MINIMUM_ALPHA); they were lit then discarded. Same image. The gain depends on the content (`AURORA_BLEND_EARLY_DISCARD=alt`, same scene, 64 lights): none on thin strands (−1%: the GPU lights fragments in groups, a group is only spared if it is entirely empty), −9% with wide strands (`AURORA_DEMO_HAIR=32,24,60,128`), −33% in SMAA (1.14 → 0.76 ms, frame 2.29 → 1.92 ms) and −35% in MSAA 4x (1.41 → 0.91 ms) with large empty areas (`32,24,90,256`).
    - identical image, verified: `AURORA_LIGHT_TILES=check` makes the shaders paint in magenta any fragment reached by a light of the list that is not in its sets — no pixel in six demo screenshots (the plaza alone, the crowd and 64 lights seen from the front and from the middle, in MSAA 4x and in SMAA), 954,000 when the lights' radius is deliberately reduced by 40% in the sort; test of the sort along the view rays (`light_tiles.rs`). Cause, measured with the new `s_*` detail of the profile: the upload of decoded textures, up to 24 MB per frame through `Queue::write_texture`, which copies the data on the main thread (~9 GB/s, i.e. 2.5 to 6 ms, and a staging buffer created per mip level: thousands of calls for small textures), with no priority order; task results applied for up to 6 ms per frame (picking copy and per-bone bounds computed and geometry written on the main thread); the J2C data copied for each decode and, every 2 s, for each cache write, one task launched per texture; the skin bindings resent in full for each rigged mesh; for `complexity`, the path and profile of the four LODs regenerated for each worn prim (1 to 3 µs per prim). Fixed: the background tasks themselves write mips, vertices and indices into a mapped staging memory, created once (`aurora-render/src/upload.rs`, 8 × 32 MB, one task at a time: 30 simultaneous writes into write-combined memory froze all the threads for 16 ms; a task waits for a free chunk rather than leaving the copy to the main thread); the main thread only records the GPU copies, in an encoder submitted at the head of the frame (page compaction and arena growth go through it too, for the order of the copies), with a per-frame budget (5% of the frame, at least 0.8 ms for textures and 1 ms for task results, at most 3 ms; 24 MB copied by the GPU) and a priority: textures still on their placeholder first, then the largest on screen, a coarse level skipped when a finer one is waiting (Firestorm creates its textures within 2 to 5 ms per frame, `LLViewerTextureList::updateImagesCreateTextures`); J2C data shared, cache reads and writes queued in one go; skin bindings: only the appended tail; background tasks at low priority (they were taking cores from the frame's threads); triangle counts of prims kept per shape. Remaining: a texture page created on the main thread costs 0.4 to 0.9 ms when wgpu's allocator takes a new block of video memory, and sometimes 3 to 10 ms (measured before as well as after, video memory under load; beyond 4 ms the log reports it, `s_pages` in the profile). To verify on Agni (BackBone Main Store): arrival, camera turned fast in the shop, teleport; `stream` and `results` out of `max:` or around 1–2 ms, `s_upload` / `s_geometry` / `s_maintain` / `s_skin` for what would remain, `slow=`; textures that arrive as fast as before, media and avatars unchanged — validated on Agni on 2026-10-10: `stream` max 3.4 ms in median and 6.8 ms at the 90th percentile during loading (instead of 10–24 ms), `complexity` no longer exceeds 1 ms, all the uploads go through the buffers (0 direct upload), nothing missing on screen

Causes, reproduced and measured in demo: (1) **memory freed on the main thread** while the tasks allocate on all the cores (the heap serialises large blocks): in `s_upload`, the GPU copies took only 0.01 to 0.2 ms, but freeing the decoded levels kept for the interface (≤ 256 px) took 1 to 3.4 ms for a handful of uploads, out of the budget's sight; in `s_maintain`, the J2C data of the evicted textures: 64 ms for 6,000 textures, 203 ms for 12,000 (the 65 ms spike on Agni: the textures of the region left, 45 s after a teleport); (2) `maintain` walked all the textures every 2 s; (3) `sync` did all the full syncs in the arrival frame (~1.2 µs per object: 5 to 16 ms for 9,000 to 12,000 objects), the mirror of the draw records was copied in full at each doubling (1.2 then 2.3 ms at 16,000 and 32,000 records, then resent in full to the GPU in `render`), each texture met for the first time wrote its 1×1 placeholder through `write_texture` (1.3 µs: 16 ms for 12,000), all the faces were reclassified at each alpha class change (0.4 to 0.6 ms for 54,000 faces, in most frames of the loading) and the removed objects were freed all at once (2.7 ms for 6,000); (4) `s_geometry`: a chunk of staging memory that became copyable placed all its geometry in the same frame (outside the budget), and the arena allocator (first fit) walked its holes: 9 to 14 µs per allocation with ~10,000 holes, twice per face; (5) `render`: an emptied texture page costs ~0.4 ms to destroy; they went together when the bind group was rebuilt (1 to 4 ms during resolution increases) and, for a region left, in one submission of 50 to 109 ms. Fixed: memory returned by a separate thread (`Jobs::discard`: decoded levels, download bodies, data of evicted textures, picking triangles); eviction through a queue in the order of the frees, 64 textures per frame at most, cache writes noted when the data arrives (no more pass over all the textures in `maintain`); uploads not yet copyable kept out of the priority heap; full syncs within a time budget (the share of the frame given by `frame_share`, 1 ms at 185 fps, 8 ms behind a loading or teleport screen): the rest waits in a queue served from nearest to the camera to farthest (`Backlog`, `FullSyncBudget`; avatars and moves always applied, the already displayed faces of a waiting object keep following it); removed objects freed within the same budget; draw records kept in 1 MB blocks and GPU buffer grown by a GPU copy; shared grey placeholder (no GPU work for a waiting texture); alpha reclassified only for the faces of the textures that change class (slot → objects index); task results bounded for the three kinds (geometry that became copyable, downloads, finished tasks); best-fit arena through an index of sizes (0.2 µs per allocation); emptied pages destroyed by a separate thread, one every 4 ms; scene and texture tables sized for a busy region. New readings: `s_sync_list` / `s_sync_plan` / `s_sync_apply` / `s_sync_alpha` and `sync_backlog` in "perf summary". Frames identical before / after apart from particles and clock (demo, 9,000 textures with and without renewal, stream, animesh, texture animations, crowd, PBR, planar, actions, occlusion), GPU validation with no error; tests: queues (eviction, uploads, syncs), budget, allocator, blocks, and two GPU tests (`cargo test -p aurora-render -- --ignored`: records across two growths, shared placeholder). The texture upkeep mentioned in the "regular spikes, later" line is therefore settled. To verify on Agni (BackBone Main Store): arrival, camera turned fast, teleport there and back (45 s later, no more spike); `max:` without `s_maintain`, `s_upload` apart from page creation (`s_pages`), `sync` around 1–2 ms with `sync_backlog` falling back to 0 in a few frames, objects that appear from nearest to farthest with no visible delay, textures and media unchanged — validated on Agni on 2026-10-10: `s_maintain` no longer exceeds 1 ms, `s_upload` 2.0 ms in median and 3.9 ms at worst (instead of 3.2 and 8.1), `stream` 2.4 ms in median; loading judged smooth, nothing missing

Fixed (`scene/hover.rs`): the sync keeps a compact index of the bounding spheres; one pass over this index gives the candidates (close to the cursor ray, or around the depth point read on the GPU, which lags by a frame or two on a moving cursor), and the exact tests of `picking.rs` (triangles, click actions, transparency, IGNORE) run only on them, in the same order: same answer as the full search. The answer is kept as long as the ray, the depth point and the surrounding objects do not change (the index reports any object added, removed, moved by more than 2 mm or modified near the ray; anything drawn that moves changes the depth), and redone at least every 100 ms (animated attachments, avatar sitting down, root of a linkset changing). Cursors, hover requests (`hover_request`) and targets re-evaluated every frame on the object found; clicks never read this answer (full search, blocking pick, unchanged). `AURORA_HOVER_CHECK=1` compares each answer with the full search and logs the differences; `AURORA_DEMO_HOVER=1` sweeps the cursor then leaves it still. Check: no difference over ~20,000 searches (actions demo, 9,000 cubes, crowd + animesh, object stream), no stale kept answer; `AURORA_DEMO_ACTIONS` modes (17): same click logs as before. To verify on Agni: touch / sit / buy cursors at the same places as Firestorm, still cursor on an object that moves or becomes clickable (change in less than ~0.1 s), identical fps with and without Ctrl or Shift, `hover` ≈ 0 in "perf summary"; if needed a session with `AURORA_HOVER_CHECK=1` (`hover check` lines) — validated on Agni on 2026-10-10: `hover` 0.01 ms per frame in median, cursor shapes and clicks unchanged

Reproduced in demo with the crowd of a club (`AURORA_DEMO_CROWD=52,200` + `AURORA_DEMO_ANIMESH=1`: 52 dancing avatars, 13,478 objects including 10,450 worn rigged meshes, 104 of them with a touch script, transparent faces and 20,000 triangles; `AURORA_DEMO_HOVER="x,y"` puts the cursor on a pixel) and quantified by the new `hover summary` line of the profile (searches done and why, candidates, time per step, exact tests). Three causes, all measured. (1) The search is redone every frame: on a dancer the depth read under the cursor changes every frame, and next to one it is the spheres of the avatars and of what they wear that move by more than 2 mm per frame near the ray (160 searches per second instead of 10). (2) Each search costs 0.6 to 0.9 ms: avatars and rigged meshes are tested whatever the ray (their bounds are those of the wearer, not those of the triangles tested), so all of them were candidates of the three steps of the search every time (0.45 + 0.15 ms), and a rigged mesh with a script and transparent faces whose box crosses the ray had all its triangles tested (71,000 triangles per search on a dancer, +0.25 ms). (3) Even before this search, the HUD pick walked all the objects of the scene every frame as soon as HUDs are displayed (0.10 ms for 13,500 objects, which, scaled to the 24,880 objects of the reading, would give its plateau of 0.17 to 0.22 ms: assumed, not verified on the grid). Fixed without changing the answers: (a) a class per object that is tested whatever the ray (`scene/hover.rs`), established from the object itself at the first search that follows its arrival or a change (simulator update, faces rebuilt, alpha class of a texture, change of wearer; the objects modified and the textures reclassified since the last sync are re-read before each search): IGNORE, transparent face, avatar or worn mesh; each step only receives the objects whose class lets them into it (a dressed avatar means hundreds of objects that enter none), a search that meets an IGNORE object takes all the candidates again as before, and an object excluded from all the steps can move near the ray without causing the search to be redone; a rotating check (16 classes per search) repairs within a few seconds a class that the index would not have known to be stale (`repaired` counter, stayed at 0); (b) the triangles of large faces (≥ 512 triangles, mesh and sculpts) arranged in a bounding volume hierarchy (`scene/pick_accel.rs`), built by a background task the first time the hover tests the face, with the same per-triangle computation as the full test (`pick::ray_triangle`, shared): same distance to the bit, a few dozen triangles tested instead of all; clicks and the full control search still test every triangle; (c) the HUD pick now only looks at the HUD objects listed by `build_huds` for the frame. `AURORA_HOVER_LEGACY=1` searches as before, `ab` alternates the two ways every second in the same session. Demo above, release, 160 fps, old → new way alternated every second (medians of 23 to 24 seconds, two consistent series), search time per frame: still cursor on a dancer 0.88 → 0.088 ms (longest search of each second 1.14 → 0.14 ms, ≥ 1 ms in 23 seconds out of 23 → 0 out of 24; in SMAA 0.84 → 0.082); still cursor on the ground next to the crowd 0.043 → 0.006 ms (one search every 100 ms: 0.65 → 0.083 ms each); cursor swept half the time 0.50 → 0.054 ms; HUD pick 0.101 → 0.002 ms per frame. `hover` step of "perf summary", whole passes alternated (3 of each), cursor on a dancer: 0.83 / 0.83 / 0.94 → 0.08 / 0.08 / 0.18 ms (last pair taken while the machine was under load), present in `max:` 24 to 25 seconds out of 25 → 0, 0 and 4. Without a crowd, nothing changes: 9,000 cubes 0.013 → 0.013 ms, crowd of 40 avatars 0.012 → 0.008 ms. Check `AURORA_HOVER_CHECK=1` (which now also verifies the spheres of the index and the classes against the scene at each search): no difference, no stale kept answer, no wrong sphere or class over ~22,600 searches — club (cursor on a dancer, on the ground, swept with HUDs and SMAA), crowd of 40, actions (including an IGNORE screen in front of an object: 58 searches through this path), 9,000 cubes, object stream with crowd, animesh changing mesh. Tests: classes (candidates of each step, forgetting, queue, rotating check), search with classes against the full search on a scene with a rigged mesh (opaque, then transparent with a script, then IGNORE), hierarchy against the test of every triangle over 7,500 rays (arbitrary, planar and repeated triangles, rays from close up, from 2 km and along the axes), hierarchy built then used by the hover. What remains per search in this demo (0.09 ms): the pass over the index (0.025 ms for 13,500 objects) and the worn rigged meshes with transparent faces and a touch script, whose rest-pose box is tested at each search (~0.5 µs each, 104 here). Firestorm does not test worn rigged meshes on hover or on left click (`LLVOVolume::lineSegmentIntersect`, `pick_rigged` false in `LLToolPie`): excluding them here too would remove this remainder, but would change answers (such a mesh can today hide from the hover the object behind it); not done, to be decided. Not handled either: `build_huds` still walks all the objects every frame to list the HUDs (`extras` step, not `hover`). To verify on the grid at the same place: still cursor on a dancing avatar, on the ground between avatars, then swept, HUDs worn; `hover` of "perf summary" and its presence in `max:`, `hover summary` lines (`searches`, `ms_per_frame`, `see_through`, `tested`, `triangles`, `repaired` at 0), touch / sit / buy cursors at the same places as before, HUD buttons; if needed a session with `AURORA_HOVER_LEGACY=ab`, and one with `AURORA_HOVER_CHECK=1` (no `hover check` line apart from the count every ten seconds). The position of the cursor during this session is not known: the four positions listed above remain to be tested on Agni, with the touch / sit / buy cursors and the HUD buttons
  - ✅ render thread (Agni reading 2026-10-10, BackBone Main Store: frame limited by the CPU, 5.4–6.5 ms per frame for 2.2 ms of GPU, of which `render` 1.5–2.5 ms on the main thread): a frame now costs the longer of the main thread and the render thread, and not their sum. The `Renderer` is split into two halves. Main thread (`aurora-render/src/main_thread.rs`): the stores of the scene (records and face table, object table of the culling, geometry arena, texture pages, palettes, skin bindings, staging memory), which no longer write into the GPU queue but into the frame's journal (`writes.rs`: writes and submissions replayed in order). Render thread (`renderer.rs`, `Backend`): surface, pipelines, targets, passes, egui, readbacks; it alone uses the queue. At the end of the frame the main thread hands over a self-contained packet (`packet.rs`: journal, copies in transit and chunks of staging memory to remap after the submission, handles of the scene's buffers as they are for this frame, camera and environment, CPU lists, egui primitives and textures, window size / vsync / settings, hovered pixel, screenshot) and goes straight on to the next frame. Rendezvous handover (`render_thread.rs`): a single packet at a time, none queued; if the render is late the main thread waits (no latency added beyond the pipeline). The frame that carries a screenshot is waited for (same frame captured as before); the depth of a click is read after the current frame; hover, culling counters and GPU timers come back with the frame's result (one frame later). Resizing, minimising, vsync and settings follow the packet; if the render thread disappears, every wait ends and the viewer closes. `finish`: two persistent helper threads (`helpers.rs`) instead of two threads created every frame, the third encoder finished at the same time (`r_finish` 0.50–0.70 → 0.26–0.37 ms, in both modes). `AURORA_RENDER_THREAD=0` executes the same packet on the main thread. Profile: segment `thread=on|off packet wait_render rt_frame rt_idle`, `journal_kb`, the `r_*` are those of the render thread; Performance window: "Render thread" line. Tests: order of the journal and frames that do not get mixed, rendezvous (one packet at a time, back-pressure measured, dead thread or closing without blocking), helper threads, copy of the packet's lists, choice of the screenshot; the 6 GPU tests (`cargo test -p aurora-render -- --ignored`) go through the journal. Demo, release, medians of 3 to 4 alternated passes, before → `AURORA_RENDER_THREAD=0` → render thread: crowd of 40 avatars + animesh (limited by the CPU) frame 2.90 → 2.81 → 1.87 ms (345 → 356 → 534 fps), p95 3.42 → 3.31 → 2.14, max 4.10 → 3.91 → 3.26, render thread 1.13 ms per frame which waits for the main one 0.75 ms, `wait_render` 0.00; standard demo 1.31 → 1.12 → 1.00 ms (then limited by presentation), main thread work 1.21 → 0.99 → 0.55 ms; 9,000 cubes (41,300 draws, limited by the GPU at 2.33 ms: frame unchanged, 2.4 ms) main thread work 2.25 → 1.93 → 1.40 ms, render thread 0.77 ms; streaming in waves (`AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=3000`) during loading average frame 2.29 → 1.78 → 1.48 ms, p95 3.62 → 2.92 → 2.38, worst frame 21 → 23 → 16 ms; all at once (`3000,3000`) 1.61 → 1.71 → 1.41 ms, p95 3.29 → 3.19 → 2.46, worst frame unchanged (37 → 40 → 37 ms, the arrival of the objects); loading time and GPU time unchanged. Verified in demo, render thread active and `AURORA_RENDER_THREAD=0`: no wgpu error (`AURORA_GPU_VALIDATION=1`) on standard demo, crowd with and without animesh, 9,000 textures with and without renewal, streaming, occlusion, prim and parcel media, transparency / wireframe / selection, texture animations, particles, CPU culling, no AA / TAA / SMAA; screenshots identical to before apart from particles, animation phase and clock; clicks, hover, right-click menu, Alt camera, building, demo teleports, inventory photo and multi-frame screenshots identical to before; resizing, burst of sizes, minimising and restoring driven by script; closing the window during loading, a teleport, a streaming burst; 4 min 25 s of streaming + crowd + media (110,000 frames, stable memory). To validate on Agni (BackBone Main Store, window in the foreground): fps with `AURORA_RENDER_THREAD=0` then by default, `wait_render` / `rt_idle` / `rt_frame`; resizing, minimising, alt-tab, full screen; teleports; clicks and hover; photos; media; closing during a loading. Remeasured on top of the loading smoothness work (same method: that work alone → `AURORA_RENDER_THREAD=0` → render thread): crowd + animesh frame 3.49 → 3.31 → 2.25 ms (287 → 302 → 444 fps), p95 4.08 → 3.88 → 2.61; `AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=12000,12000,leave` during loading average frame 4.08 → 3.83 → 2.61 ms, p95 6.31 → 5.90 → 4.35, loaded in 5.2 → 5.1 → 4.4 s; after leaving the region frame 2.00 → 1.77 → 1.04 ms, p95 2.89 → 2.63 → 1.57, `s_maintain` still under 1 ms; in the second when the emptied pages are destroyed, worst frame 6.4 → 9.9 → 6.4 ms: there the render thread contends with `aurora-pages` on the allocator (`r_resources` 2.9 ms and `r_submit` 1.7–1.9 ms at worst, `wait_render` 3 ms), with no extra cost for the main thread. The growth of the record buffer (copy on the GPU) goes through the journal like the rest — validated on Agni on 2026-10-10 (BackBone Main Store, window in the foreground): 343 fps in median (2.93 ms per frame) instead of ~205 (4.93 ms) that same morning without the thread, `render` 0.03 ms on the main thread, `wait_render` 0 in median, `rt_frame` 2.67 ms, GPU 2.2 ms; no defect reported, no error in the log
  - ✅ creation of texture pages with no hitch on the main thread (`s_pages`: 1.0 to 1.6 ms in one frame of the demo, it was what remained of `s_upload`; at times 3 to 10 ms on the grid). Measured first (wgpu 30, gpu-allocator, RTX 4090): a page carved out of a block of video memory that the device already holds costs 1 to 6 µs; the whole cost comes from the page that makes the allocator take a new block (128 then 256 MB, `vkAllocateMemory` under the allocator's lock: 0.5 to 1.6 ms, sometimes much more). Smaller blocks (`MemoryHints::Manual`, 64 MB) were tried and rejected: each block costs less (longest creation 1.3 → 0.55 ms alone), but they come round more often, and in the viewer the `r_resources` step of the render thread got longer at worst (1.3 → 4.8 ms, median of 3 passes). Fixed: the `aurora-pages` thread, which already destroyed the emptied pages, also creates those of the streaming textures. Before each upload, the streamer asks whether the layer is there (`TextureTable::prepare_page`); otherwise the page is requested from the thread and the upload waits a frame (at most 16 uploads set aside per frame, the other sizes go through). So as not to wait a frame per page (at 60 fps, a 2048² texture fills a page), the next page of a size is requested in advance as soon as the uploads queued for that size (counted per size in the upload queue) exceed the remaining layers, one page ahead at most per size; an advance page that nothing claims any more is destroyed after 2 s. Fallbacks: thread not started, page not arrived within 1 s or table full → creation in place as before. Log: "texture pages N by the page thread … / M by the main thread" in `demo stream: fully loaded` and in the `streaming:` line every 30 s; `s_pages` now only counts the pages created by the main thread. Tests: rule of the advance page, requests in progress (one per size, given up after 1 s), key of a regular chain, count of queued uploads per size, and a GPU test (`cargo test -p aurora-render page_thread -- --ignored`: wait for the first page, next page ready before the end of the first, textures read back at each level, unused page destroyed); the 9 GPU tests of the renderer pass. Demo, release, alternated passes before → after. `AURORA_DEMO_STREAM=3000` (5 passes): worst frame of `s_pages` 1.01 ms in median (up to 1.41, ≥ 1 ms in 3 passes out of 5) → never at 1 ms; `s_upload` 1.12 ms → under 1 ms; `stream` 1.16 ms → under 1 ms (one pass at 1.03); pages created by the main thread 218–221 in 16–18 ms → 2 (those of startup) in 0.1 ms, 214–218 by the page thread in 17–18 ms (the longest 1.0 to 1.4 ms); loading 8.80–8.83 → 8.80–8.82 s. All at once (`3000,3000`, 3 passes): `s_pages` 1.04 ms (up to 3.03) → under 1 ms, `s_upload` 1.41 (up to 3.20) → under 1 ms, loading 2.19–2.23 → 2.17–2.25 s. At 30 fps (`AURORA_FPS_LIMIT=30`, `3000,3000`): loading 20.0–21.7 → 20.0–20.3 s, 19 unused advance pages out of 249. 12,000 objects at once then region left: 700 pages by the thread, 2 by the main thread. Limit, measured: the render thread still contends with `aurora-pages` on the allocator's lock (each of its writes into the queue allocates a staging buffer); its worst steps do not move beyond the measurement noise (`r_resources` 1.01 → 1.15 ms, `r_submit` 1.52 → 1.89 ms, `rt_frame` 7.15 → 7.70 ms, medians of 5 passes; `3000,3000`: `r_resources` 1.66 → 1.38, `r_submit` 3.18 → 2.54), and the longest frame of each second, which the render thread decides in this demo, does not change (5.8 → 6.0 ms). Screenshot of the loaded demo with `AURORA_GPU_VALIDATION=1`: no wgpu error. To verify on Agni (BackBone Main Store): arrival, camera turned fast, teleport there and back; `s_pages` absent from `max:`, `s_upload` and `stream` lower than before, textures that arrive as fast, nothing grey that stays, `streaming:` line with almost all the pages "by the page thread" — validated by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12 (BackBone Main Store, 171 s of profile, 9,635 textures, 403 pages): `s_pages` absent from `max:` during the whole session, 392 pages created by the page thread and 1 by the main thread (the startup one), no page of more than 4 ms, no direct upload; during the 61 seconds when pages arrive, `s_upload` reaches 1 ms in 9 seconds and 2.98 ms at worst (reading of 2026-10-10: 2.0 ms in median, 3.9 ms at worst), `stream` 3.48 ms at worst

"GPU time per pass" panel added (timestamps between passes) to measure on the grid with / without at the same place; if the cost exceeds the gain outdoors: automatic disabling when almost nothing is hidden. Test scene: AURORA_DEMO_OCCLUSION=1 (wall + 360 objects behind): 185 draws hidden out of 451, frames identical, scene 0.80 instead of 0.84 ms GPU but total identical (1.22 / 1.20): with the depth prepass, a hidden object only costs its vertices; real gain only for hidden objects that are very heavy in triangles. To measure on the grid indoors / in a dense region with the "GPU time per pass" panel. Leads: use the visibility (read one frame later) to avoid downloading the textures of hidden objects (like LL), not animate / skin hidden avatars, and apply it to probe captures → done with the GPU lists, see the next line
  - ✅ occlusion enabled by default (like Firestorm's UseOcclusion; setting renamed `occlusion_culling` so that saved preferences take the new value, amber triangle removed; `AURORA_OCCLUSION=0|1` to force): with the GPU lists, its CPU cost per draw disappears (no more list of tests built on the CPU), the Hi-Z test of the main bins is done on the GPU, and the prepasses of the two phases now only draw their own draws (compacted lists: what was visible in the previous frame, then what has become visible again) instead of walking all the bins with instance_count at 0. Demo (release, medians of 4 passes): 9,000 cubes including 21,800 hidden draws GPU 3.09 → 2.76 ms (prepasses 1.32 → 1.16, objects 0.89 → 0.73) for +0.04 ms CPU; scenes where almost nothing is hidden: +0.03 to +0.06 ms GPU and ~+0.06 ms CPU (finish), so no automatic disabling. The CPU path keeps the old occlusion. To compare on Agni with / without (Graphics › Quality "Occlusion") — validated on Agni on 2026-10-10: 1,280 draws hidden out of 3,408 at BackBone, with no loss (scene limited by the CPU: GPU 2.2 ms for 6.4 ms per frame); kept by default

Reminder: Firestorm's occlusion (UseOcclusion) is active by default, ours not as long as it is not finished, which weighs in the fps gap measured at BackBone Main Store (Firestorm ~126 fps, Aurora ~50). The per-texture cost of finish() is handled differently by the texture pages (Perf section) — Re-evaluated: the bindless array now only contains the pages (~400 at BackBone Main Store, finish 0.84 ms measured on Agni), the per-texture cost has disappeared; binding only the recently seen textures would no longer bring anything and would risk flickering: not done

Reading on Agni on 2026-10-13 (dev, no fps limit, medians of the "perf summary" lines; skybox with 11,600 objects, busy region with 22,900, peak of 33,800 objects with both):

Same thing the other way: the objects of the skybox stayed 50 s in the busy region;
  - **afterwards, 838 → 555 fps** (1.20 → 1.80 ms) with the same number of objects as at the start: `lists` +0.43 ms (`Scene::build_lists` walks all the object slots ever used; neither `ObjectStore::slots` nor `Scene::gpu` shrinks, and a freed slot is reused at random across the whole range), `stream` +0.20 (10,600 live textures instead of 4,300, 4.4 GB of pages instead of 0.6; `s_assets` +0.12), `sync` +0.07. Reproduced in demo (world emptied after a peak of 19,500 objects: `lists` 0.00 → 0.18 ms). The geometry memory does not come back down either (80 → 1,280 MB). The GPU (+0.5 ms) is not comparable between the two moments: the camera was not at the same place (transparent faces, shadows of our avatar).

They come back as they are (`ObjectStore::restore`: new for the scene, links and link order redone, particle system given back — `Object::particles` now keeps it), then catch up on these events, as soon as the region becomes the agent's again (`MainRegionChanged`) or comes back within range; they leave for good with the region (`RegionRemoved`) or the session. Nothing changes on the network side: these objects have to be kept, a simulator that has not closed its circuit does not resend what it has already sent (trial of 2026-10-13 on Agni with a first version that threw them away: return to KB 50 s after leaving it, only the terrain, the avatars and what they wear came back). Firestorm also keeps them until the `DisableSimulator` and only walks the regions in view. Border crossing: the region left and its neighbours are within range, nothing is set aside. Measured on Agni with the first version (same effect on fps): on the return to the skybox, 11,970 objects from arrival instead of 24,500 for 50 s, ~460 fps instead of ~320 (840 to 950 before the busy region: the rest is in the next two points). Demo scenario `AURORA_DEMO_TP_AWAY=1` (departure to 25 km away then return: same frame before and after, 57 objects restored). Validated on Agni on 2026-10-13 (skybox at altitude ⇄ KB): four returns in 11 to 41 s, 10,869 to 15,768 objects restored each time with up to 76 events caught up, whole region at once; after more than a minute, normal reload by the simulator; 11,970 objects from arrival in the skybox. Still to check on Agni: a border crossing (nothing must disappear from the region left), a set-aside region that becomes a neighbour again before it closes, and the avatars of a recovered region, which start again as new in "People" ("Seen" column)
  - ✅ object slots (`scene/list_index.rs`): `build_lists` and `build_huds` read from the `ObjGpu` of every slot, at each frame, what it takes to pick a few objects (avatars, transparent or glowing faces, slice of the texture tracking, worn HUDs): megabytes walked, for every slot used since the session began. One byte per slot now holds it, written where the GPU's object table is written (after an object's sync, when the alpha of its faces is reclassified, when its slot is freed). Same frame. Demo (dev, cap of 500 fps, medians of 2 alternated passes with `AURORA_LIST_INDEX=0`, 52 dressed avatars and 6,000 prims): world emptied after a peak of 19,500 objects, `lists` 0.16 → 0.035 ms and the main thread's work 0.62 → 0.45 ms (0.45 in a world never loaded); 13,500 objects present, `lists` 0.30 → 0.17 ms. `AURORA_LIST_INDEX=check`: no difference between the index and the objects on these scenarios, with `AURORA_DEMO_HUDS=1` and `AURORA_DEMO_TP_AWAY=1`; same draws, same transparent faces and same screenshots as with `0`. The GPU culling tables were not touched: `g_cull` does not move with the object peak (0.017 ms). Validated on Agni on 2026-10-13 with `AURORA_LIST_INDEX=check` (skybox → KB → skybox): no difference between the index and the objects, nothing abnormal in the frame; `lists` 0.11 ms in the skybox at 11,600 objects (0.14 to 0.15 before), 0.34 ms at KB with 22,900 objects (0.57 to 0.65 before), 0.21 to 0.28 ms in the 38 s that follow the return (0.45 to 0.55 before). What is left on the return no longer comes from the slots: `recompute_wants`, one frame in thirty in `build_lists`, walks the 13,700 textures still alive of the region left (4,300 at the start); that is the next item
  - ✅ meshes and materials already seen (`scene/meshes.rs`, `scene/legacy_mat.rs`): `MeshStreamer::update` and `MaterialStreamer::update` walked every mesh and material known since the session began at each frame (they are never forgotten), and `LegacyMaterials::plan` all its entries to drop the expired ones. Measured on Agni: `s_assets` 0.03 ms in the skybox at first, 0.16 to 0.18 ms for good after KB (7,757 meshes, 4,437 legacy materials, 271 glTF materials). They now only visit the entries that have work (`todo`: disk cache to read, download to start or start again, LODs to build), listed once when they get some; `plan` only looks at its entries at the first known expiry (`next_expiry`). Same order of requests, same delays. `meshes.fetching` now counts the downloads under way (`by_key`), those started in the frame included. Demo: crowd of 52 avatars wearing rigged meshes, same 7,299 draws, 873 k triangles and 57 blended faces as before. Validated on Agni on 2026-10-13 (skybox → KB → skybox): `s_assets` 0.00 ms in the skybox (2,877 meshes), 0.02 ms at KB (10,570 meshes, 4,188 legacy materials, 351 glTF materials, none pending, no new failure), 0.01 ms back in the skybox (0.16 to 0.18 before)
  - ✅ textures visited only when they have work (`scene/textures.rs`): `TextureStreamer::update` walked every texture at each frame (0.14 to 0.17 ms for 4,300 textures in a skybox at rest, about 35 ns per texture; 0.26 to 0.45 ms with the 13,700 of a busy region, which are kept 45 s after leaving it for an immediate return). It now visits a `todo` list: a texture is listed once when it has work (`Entry::has_work`: its first disk read, or a finer level than the one on the GPU to read, decode or download) and stays listed while it waits for a retry delay, a decode slot or its upload, as the walk visited it. Every change to what `has_work` reads goes through `TextureStreamer::settle`, which also keeps the counts of loaded, downloading, failing and being-read textures (they were counted by the walk). While more than half of the textures are listed (a region arriving), the table is walked in its own order, without a lookup per texture. `AURORA_TEXTURE_TODO=0` walks as before, `check` compares the list and the counts with a walk one frame in thirty. Demo (dev, 240 fps cap, old and new in the same binary): 6,000 textures kept loaded, `s_tex_update` 0.20 → 0.00 ms, loaded in 3.5 to 4.0 s either way, same image; `check` without any difference on the stream with `,leave`, the away-and-back teleport, the stress churn and `AURORA_TEXTURE_BUDGET_MB=512` / `96` (same pressure steps and same texture memory as the walk). ## Performance audit — 2026-10-13

What limits the frame rate, the smoothness, the memory and the loading time in a place full of avatars, **the most rewarding first**. Reading taken by the human on Agni on 2026-10-13: release build of `main` (`09830247`), login at KB, 84 s online (about 18,700 frames) with their own settings — 2560 × 1369, SMAA, shadows "High", SSAO, SSR, 16 full avatars, draw distance 96 m, no fps cap, no vertical sync (`Mailbox`) — on a GeForce RTX 4090 and a Core i9-14900K (8 performance and 16 efficiency cores, 32 logical), 32 GB. `AURORA_PROFILE=1` and, from outside the viewer every 1.5 s, the process memory, the CPU time of each named thread, the GPU load and the video memory per process, and `nvidia-smi`; no other viewer on the GPU during the reading. Scene: 22,900 objects of which 1,700 to 3,200 visible, 41 to 43 posed skeletons, 64 lights, 32 probes, sun at 11° (parcel environment). One PR per point, with the before / after measurement at the same place; a point that repeats an open line of "Optimisation" says so and only adds this reading.

> **Frame rate and smoothness**: median 185 fps (158 to 277 depending on the view), `p95` 6.1 ms, worst frame 27 ms (93.8 ms on the click that closes the window, known), a frame of 16.7 ms or more in 6 seconds out of 76, 1.1% of slow frames. The GPU is the limit in 50 seconds out of 76 (`gpu` = 0.99 × `rt_frame`, 93% load and 367 W according to `nvidia-smi`), the main thread in 18 (looking away from the crowd: 256 fps).
>
> **Facing the crowd, still camera** (14 s, 173 fps). GPU 5.64 ms: `g_shadows_depth` 2.20 (39%), `g_objects` 1.61 (29%), `g_effects` 0.79 (14%), `g_transparent` + `g_post` 0.91 (16%). Main thread, 3.39 ms of work: `sync` 1.38, `ui` 0.54, `poses` 0.46, `lists` 0.28, `extras` 0.27, `params` 0.23. Render thread, 2.49 ms without its waits: `r_resources` 1.23, `r_submit` 0.42, `r_finish` 0.36, `r_tessellate` 0.19, `r_egui` 0.12.

  - 🟡 opaque casters drawn in one cascade (2026-10-13): a caster whose shadow reaches two or three cascades was drawn in each of them, in a crowd every avatar. The cascades look along the same light, so the finer map already holds, inside its square, what the next cascade would have drawn there: an opaque caster that the cascade before holds (it draws it, or leaves it in turn to the one before) and that is inside that cascade's square with two texels to spare is left out of the cascade (`shadow_cull::merged_from_finer`, `cull.wgsl` and the CPU lists), and between the two cascades' draws the finer tile is copied into its part of the coarser one (`shadow_merge.rs`, `shaders/shadow_merge.wgsl`: the finer tile to a scratch map half a tile wide, since the atlas cannot be read while it is drawn into, then the scratch over the coarser tile, nearest depth kept). The finer map is read at the centre of each coarser texel, where a draw would have sampled the caster, its depth brought to the coarser cascade's range and moved back by what the slope-scaled bias of the pipelines would have added for the wider texel (the slope is read from the map). The lookup is unchanged: a pixel reads the cascade of its distance, at the resolution it had. The alpha-tested casters are drawn in every cascade as before, after the copy: a finer map cuts their texture out differently. Firestorm draws every caster in each split it reaches (`LLPipeline::generateSunShadow`). `AURORA_SHADOW_LEGACY=separate` brings the former drawing back, `merge` alternates the two.

- ⬜ **4. Hitches** (smoothness: a frame of 10 ms or more in 15 seconds out of 76, of 16.7 ms or more in 6, for a median frame of 5.4 ms).
  - ⬜ growth of the geometry arena (`aurora-render/src/arena.rs`): one vertex buffer, one skin buffer and one index buffer, each replaced when full by one twice its size. The frame waited in `r_acquire` when the vertex arena went to 384 MB (7.8 ms, 10.3 ms frame) and to 768 MB (14.3 ms, 19.6 ms frame). **Cause found on 2026-10-13, and it is not the copy**: the first use of a new buffer costs about 21 µs per MB, the whole buffer at once, whatever is done to it — fresh video memory. Measured alone on the RTX 4090 (`cargo test -p aurora-render new_buffer_first_use -- --ignored --nocapture`): 5.8 ms for 256 MB, 10.8 ms for 512 MB, 21.8 ms for 1 GB the first time, 0.2 ms the second; 32 MB copied into it, 0.2 ms. Seen frame by frame in the demo (`AURORA_DEMO_GEOMETRY=700,60`, `AURORA_PROFILE_FRAMES=1`, with the copy spread over several frames, below): the slow frame is the one after the larger buffer is first written to, not the one that starts drawing from it.
    - tried and withdrawn: the arena grown ahead of need (at 7/8 full, by half) with the copy spread over the frames, 32 MB each, the writes going to both sets of buffers meanwhile. Same stalls (8.8, 13.1 and 17.0 ms for 364, 546 and 820 MB), and more of them since it allocates more buffers; clearing the new part slice by slice, or keeping the old buffers alive, changed nothing. Doubling when full allocates the fewest buffers and stays.
    - not a risk after all: the arena does not fail at 2 GB. It stops growing at the largest buffer of the GPU (2 GB at most) and only refuses a mesh beyond about 89 million live vertices, which the log now says; the geometry of what is no longer used is freed after 600 frames and its place reused, so what counts is what one place needs (about 0.5 to 0.7 GB at KB).
    - ⬜ to make these stalls small the geometry must live in several smaller buffers (64 MB: 1.4 ms each), and a draw reads one vertex buffer: the GPU culling would have to bin the draws per buffer as well as per pass (`cull.wgsl`: 15 bins today), or the vertex shaders fetch their vertices themselves from an array of buffers. A piece of work on the scale of the GPU culling itself, for two frames per arrival: to weigh against the other hitches of a loading region (`sync`, `r_submit`, below)
    - ⬜ cheaper, for a place already visited: remember what its geometry needed and grow the arena to that size while the loading or teleport screen still covers the view. Nothing for a first visit
    - demo: `AURORA_DEMO_GEOMETRY=<mb>[,<mb per second>]` fills the arena with meshes that are not drawn, to make it grow at will

## Performance audit — 2026-10-16

The same questions an hour long, **the most rewarding first**. Reading taken by the human on Agni on 2026-10-16: release build of `main` of the day (frame pacing of #492 included) with the deep profile lines (`msg`, `http`, `asset`, `avatar`, `memory` and `cpu summary` every 10 s, teleport and region link timelines), `AURORA_PROFILE=1`, nothing else forced. Login, four teleports, then 62 minutes at KB with the camera still (the human away from the PC): preset "Deluxe", 2560 × 1369 (maximised window), no fps cap, no vertical sync (`Mailbox`), draw distance 96 m, detail factor 3, 16 full avatars, shadows on; same PC as on 2026-10-13 (GeForce RTX 4090, Core i9-14900K, 32 GB). The screen went to sleep after 29 minutes (one frame of 593 ms, all of it in `r_acquire`, then 165 to 172 fps with nothing composed on the desktop): the figures below are those of the 27 minutes before. Scene: 54 to 63 avatars (16 full, 26 to 35 impostors in view, 40 to 56 impostor pictures per second), 27,700 to 31,200 objects of which 3,300 to 3,950 visible, about 3,500 particles, about 60 posed skeletons. No region crossing in this reading. One PR per point, with the before / after measurement at the same place; a point that repeats an open line of the audit of 2026-10-13 says so and only adds this reading.

> **Frame rate and smoothness**: about 150 fps (6.7 ms), `p95` 7.3 ms; over 27 minutes (241,000 frames) one frame of 16.7 ms or more (18.6 ms), 814 of 10 ms or more (30 a minute), 141 of 12 ms or more (5 a minute), in bursts a second apart. Frame pacing (#492) holds: the geometry arena grew ahead once behind the loading screen, and its later growths in the world cost no frame over 16.2 ms.

Large GPU allocations now go through `gpu_alloc.rs` (`try_buffer`, `try_texture`: an out-of-memory or validation error scope, and a clear of the new buffer's first bytes recorded but never submitted, which makes an invalid buffer show): the geometry arena tries halfway sizes down to what the mesh needs, then keeps its buffers and says once that the meshes left over are not drawn; the draw records, the culling tables, the skin bindings and the joint palettes keep their buffer and write what fits; a texture page that cannot be made is not installed and the texture waits; each failure is tried again after 2 s, then up to 30 s apart. The growth ahead of need stays within what the video memory budget leaves free less a margin (`ahead_allowance`: a tenth of the budget, at least 512 MB) and falls back to growth on need when it fails. The uncaptured wgpu errors are written once, then every 10 s with their count. `AURORA_GPU_OOM=<mb>` makes the allocations of that size fail (docs/TESTING.md). ## Caches

- 🟡 "Refresh textures" and "Force appearance update (rebake)", Firestorm's force rez (#272, the texture half; the skeleton half is its own task). Validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-14 (`AURORA_DEMO_TEXREFRESH`, rebake menu and Ctrl+Alt+R). Object.TexRefresh / Avatar.TexRefresh / Advanced.RebakeTextures (`llviewermenu.cpp`: `destroy_texture`, `handle_object_tex_refresh`, `avatar_tex_refresh`, `handle_rebake_textures`; `llappearancemgr.cpp`: `syncCofVersionAndRefreshCoro`, `serverAppearanceUpdateCoro`). In the menus of an object, of what we wear, of what another avatar wears (that object's linkset: faces, legacy material maps, glTF maps, sculpt map), of another avatar and of ours (its bakes, then the generic `avatartexturesrequest`). `TextureStreamer::refresh` forgets the texture once no disk read, decode or download of it is under way (their result would bring the old data back), removes its `.j2c` / `.part` / `.bc7` files off the main thread and downloads it again, never from the disk; an upload decoded before the refresh is dropped (`Entry::epoch`). Rebake (Appearance menu of our avatar, Ctrl+Alt+R, rebindable): GET `IncrementCOFVersion` (5 retries, 1 to 31 s apart), the version it answers is taken as the COF's and as received, then the bake request as `requestServerAppearanceUpdate` (skipped when the server already sent that version; without the capability, the bake request alone), and our bakes are refreshed (FIRE-11800). Demo: `AURORA_DEMO_TEXREFRESH=1|auto` (stale cached picture, right one on the local asset server). Deliberate differences: the slot keeps its texels until the new ones replace them (Firestorm shows the grey placeholder meanwhile); an avatar's refresh also takes the five bakes-on-mesh slots (Firestorm the six system ones only). Not ported: `forceBakeAllTextures` (Aurora only knows server bakes), the mesh LOD reset of the rebake (its own entry, still greyed) and `setIsCrossingRegion(false)`.
  - ⬜ later: a refreshed sculpt map rebuilds the geometry only when the object is rebuilt (Firestorm calls `notifyMeshLoaded` on its volumes at once)
  - 🟡 to check on Agni: a friend left grey or blurred, refreshed; an object whose texture shows wrong, refreshed; Ctrl+Alt+R with the outfit unchanged (the log tells `Current Outfit folder version stepped to <n>`, our avatar reloads its bakes and others see it rebaked)

Routing (`app/script_clicks.rs`): in mouselook, a mouselook button taken by a script (leftButtonGrabbed) sends only ML_LBUTTON_DOWN / UP (LLToolCompGun); not taken, the object under the crosshair is touched or grabbed (no sit, pay or buy: LLToolGrabBase) and LBUTTON_DOWN / UP go out; outside mouselook, a press on the world that nothing takes (ground, an object without action, not the build tools) sends LBUTTON_DOWN / UP (LLViewerInput::scanMouse). #488: a prim we wear with a touch action takes the click before our avatar (LLToolPie::handleLeftClickPick: touchable first), where the press used to fall on our avatar and turn the camera; worn meshes already were. On an avatar the CPU search goes on 25 cm under the mesh's surface (not through the body to what is worn on the other side); behind an animesh, to the end of the ray. Rigged meshes with a script or an action keep the click (Aurora's difference, scene/drawn.rs); the right-click menu and the build tools still designate every rigged mesh. Its alpha-0 faces are now tested on the CPU (placed by its attachment point like a worn prim; its visible faces stay the GPU's, rigged meshes stay out), and an object whose faces are all at alpha 0 (no draw record) counts as see-through for the touch search: the Legacy Viewer picks the fully transparent faces of an object with a touch script or a click action (LLVOVolume::lineSegmentIntersect, specialHoverCursor). - 🟡 Clicks on what is rigged, and attachment menus like Firestorm (`aurora-render/src/drawn_pick.rs`, `scene/drawn.rs`, `app/click_pick.rs`, `ui/context/entries.rs`). Before: an animesh or a worn rigged mesh could be neither touched, nor selected, nor right-clicked — the right click opened the menu of whatever was behind (or the avatar's for what we wear), because the CPU search only knows a rigged mesh in its rest pose. Now the click reads what the GPU drew under its pixel: the frame that follows the click redraws the faces of the view through a camera narrowed onto that pixel (target of 2 × 2 texels: draw record, depth, surface coordinates; opaque and masked faces, then the transparent faces in front of them, where their texel is visible), with the scene's vertex shader, so posed as on screen. Nothing per frame outside a click. **Deliberate difference from Firestorm**: there a rigged mesh is only reached if `pick_rigged` is true — right click (`LLToolPie::handleRightMouseDown`) and Move tool (`LLToolCompTranslate`), plus our own rigged objects when the build window is open (`LLVOVolume::lineSegmentIntersect`); the left click and the hover pass `pick_rigged = false` (`LLToolPie::handleMouseDown` / `handleHover`, `AnimatedObjectsAllowLeftClick` commented out): one cannot touch an animesh or a worn rigged object there, the click goes to the avatar's collision volumes or to what is behind. In Aurora all the clicks reach them, where they are displayed; once designated, the object follows the rules of a prim of the same status (click action, touch, IGNORE, transparent face taken by a left click only if it acts on the object, rights, menus). Right click: rezzed animesh → object menu; object worn by us → `menu_attachment_self.xml`; by another → `menu_attachment_other.xml` (entries of the avatar then of the object), now a separate menu, in Firestorm's order: without "Offer teleport" or the complexity line of the avatar menu, with "Remove from display exceptions" only if there is one and "Save as ▸" (Backup, Collada, greyed); menu of our attachments completed ("Sit / stand", "Save as ▸", "Fly / Land" greyed when seated). The attachment of the menu is surrounded by the blue wireframe of the child prims of a selection as long as the menu is open (Firestorm: silhouette of the temporary selection). Touch of a rigged mesh: exact face, position, ST and UV (read on the GPU at the pixel), normal and binormal of the posed surface around the pixel (Firestorm sends those, unposed, of the rigged volume), zero at the edge of a face; a held touch keeps the surface of its press. Cost, crowd of 250 rigged avatars (14,562 objects, 120 fps): 0.3 to 0.5 ms of GPU in the frame of the click, nothing measurable otherwise (3.92 / 3.76 ms of GPU without a click, 3.94 / 3.75 with one click per second); the answer arrives one frame later than the depth alone (2 frames at a capped 120 fps). Demo: `AURORA_DEMO_CLICKS=150,rigged,menu|left|build` with `AURORA_DEMO_ANIMESH=1` (docs/TESTING.md): rezzed animesh, animesh worn by another, rigged mesh worn by us → 74 clicks designated out of 74 aimed in the open per kind of click (object menu, menu of an object worn by another, of our attachments; 74 touches; selection of the two rezzed animesh), point read on the GPU always within the posed bounds known to the CPU; with the old read (`AURORA_CLICK_PICK=wait`): menu of the platform or of the wall behind, no touch, no selection. First try by the human on Agni on 2026-10-12 (KB, same session as the hitch on click, 66 clicks: "perfect"), merge requested on this basis. Tests to complete on Agni: left click — touch of a scripted animesh, sit and buy on a rigged object, rigged mesh with opaque faces, rigged without a script (nothing must happen, a click on our avatar still steers it); right click — rezzed animesh, worn animesh, non-rigged worn prim (by us, by another), avatar with no object under the cursor, with for each the right menu, its entries wired up (Show in inventory and Detach, greyed in demo) and the blue outline; build — selection of a rezzed animesh, window open then closed; Alt-click and camera on rigged content; very brief clicks and touch held then released; delay of the click under a cap at 60 and 120 fps; left click and hover on ordinary objects unchanged

Three selection spaces never mixed, like `LLSelectMgr::canSelectObject`: world, attachment, HUD. "Touch" is only active if the root of the object reacts to touch (`enable_attachment_touch`). **Inspect** (`LLFloaterInspect`, menus of objects, of our attachments and of those of others): "Inspect Objects" window with one row per prim (the linked prims indented under the root) — name, description, owner (or "[group] (group)"), creator, faces, vertices, triangles, TMem and VRAM in KB, creation date in SLT; totals on the left (objects, prims, faces, visible faces, vertices, triangles, complexity, textures, memory); sort by click on a header (ascending, descending, linkset order); columns to tick, saved (FSInspectColumnConfig, all by default); "See Owner Profile / Creator Profile" of the highlighted row; its prim outlined in yellow in the world, the others in blue. The properties come from an ObjectSelect of the prims, released on closing without touching the build selection. Deliberate differences: rows in linkset order (Firestorm stacks them in reverse), short date, texture memory estimated from their full size (Firestorm reads the GL memory when the texture is loaded), wireframe outline. - 🟡 Animations paused while an attachment is edited (human request, 2026-10-17; `build/anim_pause.rs`, `scene/anim.rs`; validated by the human on 2026-10-17). Port of LLSelectMgr::pauseAssociatedAvatars (llselectmgr.cpp) with LLCharacter::requestPause and LLMotionController::pauseAllMotions: as long as an attachment is in the selection — from the right click that opens its menu, through "Edit" and the build window, until the selection is dropped (menu closed without editing, window closed, another object selected) — the avatar wearing it stands still, and a selected animated object pauses its own skeleton (an animated attachment both). The motions' clock stands still (head and eyes included); on release each motion goes on from the point it had reached, without jumping ahead; a motion the simulator stops during the pause goes at once, a new one waits for the end of the pause (stopMotionLocally: stop_immediate || mPaused). Local only: nothing is sent, the server and other viewers see the avatar as before; an import preview is never paused. HUD attachments pause nothing (SELECT_TYPE_HUD); the attachments of other avatars cannot be selected in Aurora, so they never pause anyone (the Legacy Viewer's right click selects them temporarily and pauses that avatar too). No setting in the Legacy Viewer: always on. Demo `AURORA_DEMO_WORN=freeze` (our avatar dances, right click at 700, Edit at 740, window closed at 1100); unit tests for the selection rule and the paused clock. Still to verify on Agni: a HUD attachment (no pause), the selection moved to another object while editing (the pause ends), the menu dismissed without Edit (the pause ends at once), several attachments selected together, editing while seated, an animesh rezzed in the world (it stands still while selected).

- 🟡 Scripted camera (`llSetCameraParams` / `llClearCameraParams`): `SetFollowCamProperties` / `ClearFollowCamProperties` from established simulator circuits, per-object parameter retention and last-activated priority stack, following Firestorm's `llfollowcam.cpp` / `llviewermessage.cpp` / `llagentcamera.cpp`. All scalar and vector properties: pitch, distance, focus offset, position/focus lag and thresholds, behindness cone/lag, explicit eye/focus and locks; Firestorm defaults and ranges, wheel zoom and entry into mouselook, Alt camera override and Escape restoration, return to the previous source or normal camera on clear, source cleanup on object/region removal and logout. Its option `FSDisableTurningAroundWhenWalkingBackwards` was missing: Preferences › Controls › Keyboard › "Walk backward without turning around" (`walk_backwards_without_turning`, off by default as there): while the walk animation is signalled, a velocity more than 120° from the facing is drawn as a step back (`world/body.rs`), for every avatar, only on this screen. Demo: with the option on, the drawn body keeps the agent heading (27°) while walking back; off, it turns to -153°. ## Interface

- ✅ Larger text sizes ([#1227](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1227); task `text-size-range`, 2026-10-28; validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-28, no grid test needed): Preferences › Appearance › Text size goes up to 2.00× instead of 1.40× (0.80× minimum kept), for visually impaired users; every interface font follows it, inventory and chat included, on top of the interface scale (up to 200 %). The Legacy Viewer stops at +2 points (FSFontSizeAdjustment, about 1.2×): a deliberate, larger range. Fixed at large sizes: the RLVa console (`widgets::above_footer`) and the notecard preview (the Save row measured) no longer grow at every frame; the Preferences sidebar cuts its labels before their count, its footer hint gives way to the buttons and Close keeps its whole label; the Conversations entries and head grow with their two lines (`widgets::two_lines_gap`); avatar initials and the AO glyph stay icon-sized. The window steadiness, Preferences height and inspector tests also run at 2.0×; `AURORA_DEMO_OPTIONS=2:text-size` cycles 0.8 / 1.0 / 1.4 / 2.0 / 1.0, and `AURORA_TEXT_SIZE=<size>` sets the size of one launch without saving it.
  - ⬜ Later (product choice, 2026-10-28): no separate chat or inventory text size (the Legacy Viewer's ChatFontSize Small → Huge); the global size covers both.
- 🟡 Chat auto-complete of names and gestures ([#980](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/980); task `chat-autocomplete`, 2026-10-26; PR [#1080](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1080)): `@` at the start of a word lists the residents of the conversation (nearby chat: within chat range; an IM: who it is with; a group chat or conference: its participants), like LLChatMentionHelper / LLFloaterChatMentionPicker; arrows choose, Tab or Enter write `@Name`, Escape closes, and the label is sent as the `secondlife:///app/agent/<id>/mention` link. `/` and a letter in the nearby chat list the matching active gestures under the existing inline completion (an Aurora addition: the Legacy Viewer completes inline only): arrows write the trigger, Enter says it, Tab keeps it. Name prediction of residents within 162 m after three letters (FSChatbarNamePrediction, FIRE-3192), on by default at the human's request (off in the Legacy Viewer). Preferences › Chat: `chat_gesture_autocomplete`, `chat_name_prediction` and `chat_mention_autocomplete`, all on. Demo: `AURORA_DEMO_MENTION=list|names`, `AURORA_DEMO_GESTURES=list`.
  - Validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-26 (mention lists, gesture list, name prediction, options).
  - ⬜ QA on the grid: a mention chosen from the list in nearby chat, an IM and a group chat, seen as a mention by another viewer.
  - ⬜ Later: the `/whisper` and `/shout` chat-type triggers (sChatTypeTriggers, completed with the gestures in the Legacy Viewer) are not supported by Aurora's chat bar.

- ✅ ":" as a synonym for "/me" ([#1202](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1202); task `chat-colon-emote`, 2026-10-27; validated by the human in demo on 2026-10-27): Preferences › Chat › `colon_emote`, off like the Legacy Viewer's AllowMUpose. A line that starts with ":" leaves as an emote on channel 0 and in the conversations (private, group, conference): ":waves" is "/me waves", ":'s here" "/me's here"; a line of three bytes or less, or a colon followed by a digit, a punctuation mark or a space (":)", ":3"), stays as it is (FSCommon::applyMuPose, before the gestures). With the option, a line starting with ":" shows us typing only with "Also when emoting" (FSNearbyChat::handleChatBarKeystroke).

- ✅ Hide the nearby chat bar when not in use ([#1009](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/1009); task `autohide-chat-bar`, 2026-10-26; PR [#1086](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1086); validated by the human in the offline demo on 2026-10-26): Preferences › Chat › "Hide the chat bar when not in use", off by default (the Legacy Viewer's `AutohideChatBar`, Chat › Typing). - ✅ Friend location actions ([#999](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/issues/999); [PR #1033](https://github.com/Aurora-Viewer/Aurora-Viewer/pull/1033); task `friend-location-999`, 2026-10-25): contact/conversation menus, both profile layouts and the friend sheet share received map rights and online status.
